text_read: Read in full from the saved text: Ch. XII 'Palming' (source lines 5025-5483), Ch. XIII 'Memory as an Aid to Vision' (5486-5916), Ch. XIV 'Imagination as an Aid to Vision' (5919-6345), Ch. XVI 'The Illusions of Imperfect and of Normal Eyesight' (6880-7269), Ch. XVII 'Vision Under Adverse Conditions a Benefit to the Eyes' (7272-7769, the sun-gazing chapter), Ch. XXIII 'Floating Specks' (9172-9380). Table of contents and a keyword pass over the rest; the other 26 chapters (refraction theory, shifting and swinging, case histories) were not read.
mode_evidence: The source documents the dispute itself. Patients palming (eyes closed and covered, all light excluded) report lights and colours 'so vivid that they seem to be actually seen with the eyes', and some could not be argued out of the belief that they saw them with their eyes. One woman was 'positive' she saw grey with her eyes. Bates classes every such appearance as an 'illusion' of an imagination out of control, on the ground that closed eyes cannot see. So: perceptual by the percipients' report, imaginary by the author's theory. He draws no line between mind's-eye imagery and seen light; for him sight, memory and imagination are one function.
onset_evidence: Everything here must be read in reverse, since Bates's goal is a perfect black and the lights are his failure condition. Read that way it is an induction report: simply closing the eyes and covering them with the palms, without pressure, produces lights and colours at once in most of his patients, and a perfect black is rare ('some never succeed in doing it until they are cured'). Stated intensifiers: poor eyesight (the worse the sight the more numerous, vivid and persistent), fatigue, hunger, anger, worry, depression, illness, pain, and above all effort, namely trying to concentrate on black and to ignore the colours, which made them 'worse and worse'. Stated extinguishers: relaxation, a remembered small black object held 'one part best', rapid mental shifting, deliberately recalling many colours in turn. He says nothing to the person who sees only black except that this is the resting state. No prerequisites; no grace or transmission language. Time scale: immediate. Ch. XVI adds that illusions of colour, multiple lights and after-images can be produced at will by straining (staring, trying to see a whole letter equally well, looking above a light and trying to see it as well as when directly regarded).

conditions.posture: Not specified in the chapters read; the figure shows a seated patient.
conditions.gaze_or_eye_position: Eyes closed, covered with the palms, fingers crossed on the forehead, no pressure on the eyeballs.
conditions.setting: Any; light fully excluded by the hands.
conditions.duration_and_schedule: A few minutes up to half an hour in the cases given; one patient palmed about twenty hours in a day. Some gain by long sessions, others begin to strain if they keep it up too long.
conditions.other: Fatigue, hunger, anger, worry, depression, illness and pain all make black harder to see, i.e. increase the lights.

phenomena: floaters (muscae volitantes), sometimes rainbow-coloured or like white bubbles
coloured or black spots after sun-gazing
sun seen red, blue, green, yellow or black

stages.label: imperfect black
stages.description: Grey, or black that holds for a few seconds and is replaced by another colour; streaks or floating clouds of grey; clouds of black moving across the field.

stages.label: lights and colours
stages.description: Flashes of light, patches of red, blue, green, yellow.

stages.label: kaleidoscopic appearances
stages.description: The most vivid end of the range, taken by the patient for real seeing; intensified by the effort to ignore them.

stages.label: perfect black
stages.description: Bates's goal: a field so black that nothing blacker can be remembered, imagined or seen. Rare; equated with perfect relaxation and cure.

what_to_do_with_light: Abolish it, and not by force. Regard it as an illusion, stop trying to ignore or suppress it, and replace it by an easy memory of black; if that fails, stop palming and work with the eyes open.
obstacles_and_fixes: Cannot see black at all: look at a black object at the distance where its colour is seen best, close the eyes and remember it, repeat until the memory seems equal to the sight, then palm while holding it; if the field is not black within a few seconds, open and look again.

Black lasts only three to five seconds: remember a smaller area (one part of the object darker than the whole), or shift mentally from one black object to another, holding each a fraction of a second.
Persistent grey field taken for real: imagine a black C on it, then two, then a multitude of overlapping C's.

Memory of black fails: run through bright red, yellow, green, blue, purple and especially white, each in its most intense shade for no more than a second, for five or ten minutes; then remember a half-inch piece of white starch and note that the background has turned black.
Colours grow worse the more they are ignored: stop palming and, eyes open, deliberately recall as many colours as possible, so that the mind wanders on purpose.
Much difficulty: drop palming until sight has improved by other means.
cautions: Effort and 'concentration' on the black defeat themselves; a patient who tried to see black only and ignore the colours went into convulsions and was under a physician for a month.
A minority only increase their strain by palming.

Sun-gazing in people with imperfect sight can give blind areas, patches of colour lasting seconds to months (one case a year or more), hours of total blindness, and inflammation; Bates insists these are always temporary and recommends the practice with 'discretion'. That reassurance is his own claim and is not accepted by ophthalmology.
interpretation: The lights are illusions of an imagination beyond the patient's control, a sign of mental strain acting on the visual centres; closed eyes cannot see, so nothing retinal is involved. Depth of black behind closed eyes is his gauge of relaxation.
practice_summary: Bates's procedure, and what it shows in reverse. Close the eyes and cover them with the cupped palms, fingers crossed on the forehead, with no pressure on the eyeballs and no light admitted. Most people do not then see black: they see grey streaks and clouds, flashes, patches of red, blue, green and yellow, up to kaleidoscopic displays that look fully seen. These are stronger with fatigue, hunger, worry, anger, illness or pain, and grow steadily worse when one tries hard to ignore them or to concentrate on blackness. Bates wants them gone: look at a black object, close the eyes, remember it easily with one small part blackest, shift lightly between black objects, and the field darkens; or cycle quickly through vivid remembered colours and then a small white patch, after which the ground turns black. Never force. For a practitioner seeking light, the report is that covered eyes yield lights readily, that strain, depletion and suppression feed them, and that relaxed attention to a small dark point quenches them. His sun-gazing advice should not be followed.

key_passages.locator: Ch. XII 'Palming', printed pp. 123-124, source lines 5056-5097
key_passages.anchor: appearances  so  vivid  that  they  seem  to  be  actually  seen
key_passages.paraphrase: Even with eyes closed and covered so that all light is excluded, patients do not see black but lights and colours, from an imperfect black to kaleidoscopic appearances that seem actually seen with the eyes. The worse the sight, the more numerous, vivid and persistent. Fatigue, hunger, anger, worry or depression make black harder to see. Reported forms: streaks or floating clouds of grey, flashes of light, patches of red, blue, green, yellow, moving clouds of black, black replaced after a few seconds by another colour.
key_passages.quote: But even with the eyes closed and covered in such a way as to exclude all the light, the visual centers of the brain may still be disturbed, the eye may still strain to see; and instead of seeing a field so black that it is impossible to remember, imagine, or see anything blacker, as one ought normally to do when the optic nerve is not subject to the stimulation of light, the patients will see illusions of lights and colors ranging all the way from an imperfect black to kaleidoscopic appearances so vivid that they seem to be actually seen with the eyes. The worse the condition of the eyesight, as a rule, the more numerous, vivid and persistent these appearances are.

key_passages.locator: Ch. XII 'Palming', printed pp. 125-126, source lines 5102-5124
key_passages.anchor: that  they  did  not  actually  see  them  with  their  eyes.  If
key_passages.paraphrase: Some patients were so struck by the vividness of the colours that no argument could convince them they were not seeing them with their eyes. They granted that other people's closed-eye lights would be illusions but held their own to be reality, until they 'demonstrated the truth' for themselves.
key_passages.quote: Some patients have been so impressed with the vividness of the colors which they imagined they saw that no amount of argument could, or did, convince them that they did not actually see them with their eyes.

key_passages.locator: Ch. XII 'Palming', printed p. 126, source lines 5126-5141
key_passages.anchor: the  memory  of  the  black  is  perfect,  the  whole  background
key_passages.paraphrase: The antidote: look at a black object where its colour is seen best, close the eyes and remember the colour, repeat until memory seems equal to sight, then palm while holding the memory. If the memory is perfect the whole field goes black; if not within a few seconds, open the eyes and look again. Note that this is a remembered colour taking over the seen field.
key_passages.quote: Then they are instructed, while still holding the memory of the black, to cover the closed eyes with the palms of the hands in the manner just described. If the memory of the black is perfect, the whole background will be black. If it is not, or if it does not become so in the course of a few seconds, the eyes are opened and the black object regarded again.

key_passages.locator: Ch. XII 'Palming', printed p. 130, source lines 5282-5301
key_passages.anchor: tried  to  see  black  only  and  to  ignore  the  kaleidoscopic
key_passages.paraphrase: Effort and concentration on the black cannot succeed. A patient who tried to see only black and ignore the kaleidoscopic colours found them growing worse the more she ignored them, went into convulsions from the strain, and needed a month's medical attendance. The fix was to stop palming and, eyes open, recall as many colours as possible, making the mind wander on purpose; after that she could palm for short periods.
key_passages.quote: A patient who tried to see black only and to ignore the kaleidoscopic colors which intruded themselves upon her field of vision, becoming worse and worse the more they were ignored, actually went into convulsions from the strain, and was attended every day for a month by her family physician before she was able to resume the treatment.

key_passages.locator: Ch. XVII 'Vision Under Adverse Conditions', printed pp. 186-188, source lines 7389-7460
key_passages.anchor: from  the  sun,  patches  of  color  of  various  kinds  and  sizes
key_passages.paraphrase: After sun-gazing by people with defective sight: blind areas, the sun seen slate, yellow, red, blue or black, and patches of colour that persist from seconds to months, in one case a year or more after a few seconds' look; also hours of total blindness and inflammation. Bates calls all of it temporary and a mental illusion, and still recommends sun-gazing with care, even focusing the sun on the eye with a burning glass. Dangerous advice.
key_passages.quote: After looking away from the sun, patches of color of various kinds and sizes may be seen, continuing a variable length of time, from a few seconds to a few minutes, hours, or even months. In fact, one patient was troubled in this way for a year or more after looking at the sun for a few seconds.

key_passages.locator: Ch. XVI 'Illusions of Imperfect and of Normal Eyesight', printed pp. 178-180, source lines 7112-7189
key_passages.anchor: The  eyes  cannot  see  when  they  are  closed;  and  if  they
key_passages.paraphrase: Bates rejects retinal fatigue as the cause of after-images: closed eyes cannot see, so anything seen then is a mental illusion showing loss of mental control. He adds that anyone can produce an after-image at will by straining (trying to see the big C 'all alike'), and multiple lights by looking above a light and trying to see it as well as when looked at directly.
key_passages.quote: The eyes cannot see when they are closed; and if they appear to see under these conditions, it is obvious that the subject is suffering from a mental illusion with which the retina has nothing to do.

confidence_note: Relevant chapters read whole. Kept as marginal because the source aims to abolish the lights and denies they are seen; its value is as a counter-instruction and as a clinician's list of what feeds and what quenches closed-eye light. Bates's physiology and his safety claims about the sun are not reliable. The observation that the lights are commoner with worse eyesight is his clinical impression only.
